sweep_summary: Two works with stress in the title, both genuinely about Luiseño word stress, neither openable: Munro 1990 (IJAL 56(2):217-250, DOI 10.1086/466151) is paywalled at U Chicago Press/JSTOR (Unpaywall's 'green OA' flag points only to the WALS refdb bibliographic record); Weinberg 1996 (CLS 32(1):379-392) is a print-only proceedings paper with no online trace beyond the Glottolog record. The best first-hand statement actually read is Hill & Hill 2019 Comparative Takic Grammar (already held by the project, eScholarship open access), sec. 3.4.4 pp. 97-99 and Rule 2 p. 185: stress the stem syllable containing the second mora (long vowel = 2 moras, coda = 1 mora), word-final syllable extrametrical, with lexical exceptions (root-initial non-derived verbs, -CV augments, stressless roots). This confirms the catalog's weight-sensitive-with-hedge coding and refines the carried Munro-1990-via-Hill-2005 rule (adds coda weight, final extrametricality, second-syllable default for light-light nouns per Munro 1990:223 as reported by Hill & Hill). Records with. Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, archive.

new_statements.quote: LU stress is complex. It features the general Takic rule of “stress the syllable containing the second mora” but with both lexical and constructional exceptionality. ... Note that the domain of stress is the stem, with the exception of a few noun stems which, when possessed, show stress on the possessive prefix. First, a closed syllable is stressed if it is initial or preceded by a short vowel. ... When the first two syllables of the stem are both open, for nouns, stress usually falls on the long vowel. If no long vowel is present, Mamet (2010:242) holds that stress is unpredictable. Munro (1990:223) notes that stress on the second syllable ... is the most common pattern for non-derived nouns.

new_statements.locator: sec. 3.4.4 'Luiseño stress', printed p. 97 (PDF p. 99); rule statement sec. 4.4.3 Rule 2, printed p. 185 (PDF p. 187)
new_statements.reading: weight-sensitive (quantity-sensitive) stress on the stem: the syllable containing the second mora is stressed, where long vowels count two moras and coda consonants one, and the word-final syllable is extrametrical (Rule 2, p. 185). So a heavy initial syllable (CVV or CVC) is stressed, otherwise the second syllable; the default for light-light nouns is second-syllable (Munro) or unpredictable (Mamet), not first-syllable. Lexical/constructional exceptions: most non-derived verbs root-initial, -CV augments and some verbs second-syllable, stressless roots throw stress to the prefix. This supports the catalog's weight-sensitive coding and its hedge; it refines the carried Munro-via-Hill-2005 'Pre-Cupeño' rule (long vowel in σ1/σ2 else initial) by adding coda weight, final extrametricality, and a second-syllable rather than first-syllable default for light-light nouns.

audit.recode_to: Keep classification weight-hedged, edge left. On re-read with Hill & Hill 2019 sec. 3.4/3.4.4/4.4.3: weight class -> moraic CVV+CVC (coda consonants count as moras generally, not only 'CVC-by-position'); rule -> 'stress the syllable containing the second mora' (= s1 if heavy, else s2), final syllable extrametrical, lexical/constructional exceptions (verbs mostly root-initial; -CV augments shift to s2; stressless roots stress the prefix); domain -> STEM (prefixes extrametrical) instead of word; secondary rule -> 'all but the rightmost stress become secondary' (Rule 12) instead of 'No information'; strength of the evidence -> opened (2019 synthesis) instead of quotation carried over second-hand from StressTyp2.
